This case study shows how a distribution center can add value. The charity kept a single central stock of supplies for its offices. Research showed that if their branches were to buy their office supplies straight from the wholesaler it would cost less and take less time. Promptly the charity chose to shut the distribution center down. In this case the distribution center was simply adding cost and not worth. It was not providing any break-bulk, storage, consolidation or value added services.

Elevated blood pressure might cause heart and vessel disease and kills more people globally than anything else. Testing is an excellent idea.
How often to test varies with your medical background. People who've got hypertension ought to test more frequently, testing two times every day until pressure is controlled and also as often as needed provided that heart health stays under watch. People with less well-known background ought to monitor less often. The bare minimum is one check per year during a visit to the doctor, yet a good device produces correct results.
The right procedure
- First empty your bladder. Second, plan your checks around your personal health status and exactly what monitoring you need. Third, lay the arm being tested on a level, firm surface with the top of the arm at the height of the chest. Keep your back upright and propped up and your legs not crossed.
- Next, pull the cuff up the arm, its lower edge beneath clothing and right above the elbow. Hold the arm level with the heart so that gravity doesn't skew the result. Finally, keep your mouth closed while you follow your monitor's manual.
- The right cuff
- A cuff that doesn't fit, whether it's oversized or undersized, produces readings that are skewed low or high. If the cuff matches two-thirds of the distance between elbow and shoulder, the result's accurate.
- The right time
- Many doctors prefer a reading right after you wake up and before breakfast. Morning readings run higher due to daytime activity and stress, which makes evening readings more accurate.
- For half an hour beforehand, skip workouts, cigarettes and drinks with caffeine. Lay the arm being tested on a level, firm surface with the top of the arm at the height of the chest. Keep your back upright and propped up and your legs not crossed.
- To get a correct reading, stay seated and motionless for no less than five minutes first. Keep your mouth closed while you follow your monitor's manual.
- The right way to track
- Record two or three measurements per session. Hypertension sufferers ought to test two times daily until pressure is controlled. Once pressure is controlled, tests can be less frequent, provided that heart health stays under watch.
- The right device
- Keep in mind that it's not the cuff that's the device; it's the whole kit and caboodle. And when you've got a good device, the results are correct. When you're interested in monitoring your blood pressure, it's not what you think it is. Besides, elevated blood pressure might cause heart and vessel disease, which kills more people globally than anything else. So testing is a good idea.

Pupils at East Otago High School (EOHS) can take Te Reo from Year 7 through to Year 10. Te Reo in Year 9 extends the groundwork laid in the junior school. The main goal of the course is to give pupils a first taste of a different language and culture. Pupils learn to present themselves and speak about family, age, birthday, place of origin and home. They learn to count up to 100 and recite the German alphabet. They are shown German daily life and culture via the Ministry of Education’s ‘Ja’ series. Besides Vocabulary and Tikanga tied to these themes, the pupils put together a simple Kupu Hou (word bank) including greetings plus easy questions on family, friends and the classroom.
In Year 10 Te Reo is optional. The course gives pupils the confidence and ability to take NCEA Level 1 through correspondence. The curriculum is organised in a more formal approach and worked from the textbooks Te Reo Take Take and Te Matapuna. Pupils learn how sentences are built and practise short conversations. The year is split up in two groups of Te Reo. The first group is centred on Matariki and the other group learns about Parihaka. In odd years the theme is Te Marae (the marae) while in even years the theme is Kai (food).
In Year 7 and 8 pupils get one Te Reo class weekly across two terms. The course runs on a cycle that alternates between odd and even years.
In the odd years, the theme is Te Marae (the marae). This is a huge theme for the school as there are strong ties kept with the nearby marae. Besides Vocabulary and Tikanga tied to these themes, pupils put together a simple Kupu Hou (word bank) including greetings plus easy questions on family, friends and the classroom.
In the even years, the theme is Kai (food). In year two pupils develop the language they learned earlier. They keep on exploring how New Zealand and German culture differ and are alike. They learn to discuss school subjects, pets, hobbies, sport, food, telling time. In addition, they keep up studying how German and New Zealand culture are alike and different. Pupils get two periods weekly all year long.

A 2018 study published in the ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing showed how to produce high-accuracy, 30-meter cropland extent maps for Australia and China using Landsat-8 imagery, a random forest classifier, and Google Earth Engine (GEE). Much earlier global land cover products used imagery at 250 meters to 1 kilometer resolution, whereas Landsat-8 revisits each location about every 16 days. Landsat-8 offers 30-meter pixels, fine enough to resolve individual fields in many agricultural areas.
The study produced a binary map distinguishing cropland from everything else, produced separately for each country and assessed against independent reference data. The output was a map distinguishing cropland from everything else, produced separately for each country and assessed against independent reference data.
China feeds a huge population from a comparatively small area of farmland, much of it in fragmented, intensively managed plots. Mapping the extent and distribution of cropland is key to understanding Chinese agriculture and managing land and water use. Australia’s vast agricultural regions are sparsely populated and include large fields, dryland farming, and irrigation concentrated in particular basins. Water allocation is a constant concern in Australia.
The two countries’ starkly different agricultural landscapes and geographies made their cropland mapping problems, in some respects, complementary. The study produced high-accuracy 30-meter cropland extent maps for Australia and China using Landsat-8 imagery, a random forest classifier, and Google Earth Engine (GEE).

A new study shows that Landsat-8, a satellite operated by NASA and USGS, can reveal the fine-grained dynamics of cropland within entire countries. Cloud cover may limit usable observations in some regions and seasons, but researchers can take advantage of repeated observations to capture cropland expansion, abandonment, and conversion to urban use.
The magic of Landsat-8 comes from combining several steps into a single computational environment, known as Google Earth Engine. Landsat-8 revisits each location about every 16 days, so the system can continually add new data to the archive hosted alongside other datasets by Google Earth Engine and run computation on Google's cloud infrastructure.

The 2018 study demonstrated that open Landsat data, a dependable machine learning algorithm, and cloud computing make field-scale cropland mapping across entire countries feasible without well-resourced agencies. The Landsat approach is straightforward. Scientists use a machine learning technique known as random forest, which copes well with many input variables, tolerates noisy data, and is relatively resistant to overfitting. The Landsat scene itself is used as a single input, and the algorithm is trained to return a simple yes/no answer: is this scene cropland?

A Kampala-based organization working in these communities is now proposing something a bit different—a network of community-run resource centers built inside or next to the neighborhoods they serve. These centers would provide poor and orphaned children with the opportunity to play, learn, eat, and receive basic health care, and offer mothers and guardians the knowledge and skills necessary to build more stable lives. The plan includes the provision of basic health care (growth monitoring, immunization follow-up, deworming, first aid, referrals to clinics and hospitals); health facilities and practitioners are also engaged in providing referrals, outreach clinics, and maternal health services. In addition to these services, the community resource centers would offer vocational and small-business skills training that would lead to more stable income and greater independence for the children. They would also offer safe-motherhood education on prenatal care, safe delivery, postnatal recovery, family planning, and newborn care—especially for young and first-time mothers—as well as nutrition training on how to feed infants and children well on a tight budget using locally available foods.
The centers would operate in a unique way to leverage community resources, as well as to provide a safe and stimulating space for learning. They would be run by members of the communities they serve, who would provide safe and stimulating spaces for learning. To do this, the centers would
- Engage local government and community structures to align the centers with public services and child-protection systems.
- Identify and involve schools and educators to support learning and ease the children’s transition into formal education.
- Involve health facilities and practitioners for referrals, outreach clinics, and maternal health services.
- Provide open drainage channels with safe and stimulating spaces for learning, and narrow lanes that double as playgrounds.
- Create spaces to learn and play, eat, and receive basic health care.
- Open the doorways to parents and guardians to provide knowledge and skills to build more stable lives.
- How do we make these community resource centers real?
The first step is to pull together a group of committed partners who share the dream and are ready to work hard to make it come true. We have great partners on the ground who are excited about the possibilities. Next, we work together to create a comprehensive, implementable plan for building the centers. We’re already in conversations with a number of organizations and even the local government about how we can best pull this off, and we’re pretty sure we’re on the right track.
There’s still a lot to do, but with your help, we can make these community resource centers a reality for the children who need them most.

JALAA is a holistic approach to community support, aiming to not only provide sustainable aid to slum children, but also empower them to lead independent lives
In Uganda, where one of the youngest populations in the world means that 77% of the population is under 30 years of age, communities are tasked with raising the next generation to be capable, responsible, and self-sufficient adults.
The challenge, however, is that these responsibilities are placed on the shoulders of a slum’s limited resources.
Take, for instance, peri-urban slums, which are overcrowded, under-served neighborhoods characterized by cramped housing and poor sanitation, with public services that are stretched thin or absent entirely.
In these neighborhoods, narrow lanes often double as playgrounds for children, who are left with little choice but to play in unsupervised environments, exposing them to the dangers of traffic, polluted water, and abuse and exploitation.
Irregular meals, paired with limited access to clinics, leave children vulnerable to malnutrition and preventable illness.
And teenage mothers, who often leave school in order to take care of their children, are left with little information about pregnancy, childbirth, or infant care.
With JALAA, these challenges could be met with community resource centers that would provide age-appropriate early learning activities that build literacy, numeracy, and social skills.
They would also offer basic health care services like growth monitoring, immunization follow-ups, deworming, first aid, and referrals to clinics and hospitals.
Children would also receive regular, balanced, nutritious meals, as well as access to safe-motherhood education to prepare them for the prenatal care, safe delivery, postnatal recovery, family planning, and newborn care they need, especially for young and first-time mothers.
Where possible, caregivers and volunteers would come from the surrounding area, which creates jobs and builds trust.
These centers would offer more than just temporary aid, however.
When programs are entirely dependent on outside funding and staff, they tend to fade when that support ends.
These centers, therefore, would partner with schools and educators to support learning, and ease the transition into a formal education.
These centers would sustain themselves through community support, ensuring that the next generation in Uganda is given the tools to succeed.

A beautiful little Perthshire town on the banks of the River Tay, Dunkeld dates largely from the twelfth to fifteenth centuries. In 1689, after the Battle of Killiecrankie, Jacobite Highlanders and the Cameronian regiment fought in Dunkeld and much of the town burned. After this, the cathedral choir remained in use as the parish church, while the ruined nave stood beside it. Dunkeld is an important ecclesiastical centre in early medieval Scotland, and the cathedral's present form dates largely from the twelfth to fifteenth centuries.
The centre of Dunkeld has whitewashed cottages with neat gables, and a cathedral by the water. The Atholl seat was Blair Castle, to the north of Dunkeld, and the Murrays held land across this part of Perthshire for centuries. The 4th Duke of Atholl, known as the ‘Planter Duke’, planted vast numbers of larches and other conifers across Atholl lands. His great act of public service to Dunkeld was bringing piped water to the town.
When Telford's bridge across the Tay was completed in 1809, the 4th Duke of Atholl was a powerful presence in the district. It is perhaps no surprise that the people of Dunkeld chose a fountain, a structure that delivers water, as the memorial to the Duke rather than a statue. The Atholl Memorial Fountain dates from 1866, commemorating George Murray, 6th Duke of Atholl, who died in 1864.
Standing in the middle of the square, the stone fountain is a beautiful testament to the gift of the Atholl estate, the water running to the homes of Dunkeld. A suggested visit starts at the fountain, then follows the streets down to the cathedral and Telford's bridge, taking less than an hour.

Dunkeld is a town like any other, the houses scattered, the roads twisting up and down from the crossroads at the bottom of the hill. But this place has its secrets.
Visitors come here for the cathedral, the river walks and the wooded hills. But they often end up staring at the Atholl Memorial Fountain, situated at the spot where the most famous of these roads intersects with the road to Blairgowrie. It stands as a focal point today, a place to meet, pause or photograph. Yet the people of Dunkeld chose something to deliver water instead of a statue to memorialise their 4th Duke of Atholl. A ducal family could affect the housing and the village school in this small town. Relationships were unequal, as so much depended on the goodwill of one family.
The Atholl seat was Blair Castle, to the north of Dunkeld, and a powerful presence in the district when Telford completed the bridge across the Tay in 1809, replacing the ferries and giving the town a lasting connection to the south.
The estate played a leading part in the rebuilding, and later improvements, of the town. The stewardship of the cathedral grounds was one way to preserve this important site, but the water running to its homes was a gift of the Atholl estate. A ducal family’s decisions could affect people’s housing and the village school.
Dunkeld has always depended on wells, springs and the river for its water. A reliable piped supply was one of the most significant improvements a Victorian community could receive, reducing drudgery and the risk of disease.
The fountain dates from 1866 and stands as a reminder of the Atholl estate’s stewardship, the Little Houses hint at the more modest vernacular architecture of the post-fire town. Telford’s bridge across the Tay is one of the most photographed views in the area, with the cathedral and river behind it.
The Atholl family are also remembered for their plantations, transforming the look of the hills and becoming part of the area’s identity. They draw walkers and visitors. They are a legacy of the “Planter Duke”, known as the 4th Duke of Atholl, who was a powerful presence in the district when the bridge was built. A paternal responsibility of this kind was common among nineteenth-century Scottish landowners.

A non-profit organization supplied office products to its member agencies: paper, pens, toner, folders, and similar staples. Suppliers shipped these products to the center, which stored them and picked orders to ship them to the agencies. The agencies received the same products they could have received directly from the supplier, but later and at higher cost.
To see whether a distribution center would add value, consider these five tests (click link to read more detail on each):
- Consolidation: The center did not combine goods from many distant sources in a way that cut freight costs
- Break-bulk: Goods arrived in quantities the customer already liked
- Storage: The center failed storage because inventory turned over quickly and demand was steady
- Customization: There was no on-site value-added work
- Information: The center’s information function was not needed on its own (it could run through suppliers or software) and failed because the center added a handling step—every item was received, put away, picked, packed, and shipped a second time. That extra handling meant extra labor, extra space, extra inventory on the balance sheet, and extra days in lead time.
The sensible answer was elimination: have suppliers ship directly to agencies, or use a distributor that already offers consolidated delivery. The non-profit could then focus on negotiating prices and coordinating service.

The normal blood pressure for most adults is below 120/80 mm Hg.
Taking your blood pressure at home allows you to track your levels over time. This can help your doctor diagnose high blood pressure or keep track of your condition when you have a diagnosis.
People with high blood pressure, especially those over age 40, can benefit from occasional checks. If you have a diagnosis, measure your blood pressure for about seven days before a medical appointment or after a medication change. It’s a good idea to seek urgent medical attention for a reading of 180/120 or higher, especially if you have chest pain, shortness of breath, a severe headache, vision changes, weakness, or difficulty speaking.
When your blood pressure is well controlled and stable, many people check a few times a week or do a one-week round about monthly.
If you don’t have a diagnosis but are at risk, do occasional checks. You’re at risk if your family has high blood pressure, you have diabetes, or you’re overweight or have kidney disease.
For adults without a diagnosis but especially over age 40 or who have these risk factors, it’s a good idea to do occasional checks. For example, a week of readings every few months, or whenever a clinic reading is high, is a reasonable approach to take for a proactive adult. The bottom edge of the cuff should sit about an inch above the bend of the elbow, with tubing running along the inside of your arm.
Measure twice a day, morning and evening, with two readings each time, one minute apart. Sit quietly for at least five minutes before measuring — don’t talk, scroll your phone, or watch something stressful. Wait at least 30 minutes after caffeine, smoking, exercise, or alcohol before measuring. If your reading is very high without symptoms, rest for five minutes and measure again; if it’s still that high, contact your doctor promptly.
Many guidelines suggest discarding the first day’s results and averaging the rest. However, small errors can add 10 points or more to your reading, so it’s important to take two readings one minute apart and record both, with the date and time.

The home blood pressure monitor has changed the way that you monitor blood pressure. With consistent timing, rest and correct sitting, right cuff size, and record keeping, this device becomes a tool that will protect your heart, brain, and kidneys.
Home blood pressure monitoring frequency and technique
Blood pressure is measured at the elbow. Place the cuff around your bare skin, not over your clothing. The cuff should be placed on the elbow, with the tubing running along the inside of the arm, so the bottom edge is about an inch above the bend in the elbow.
- Make sure your sleeve is not acting as a tourniquet when you roll it up. This can falsely elevate blood pressure.
- Sit in a chair with a back and sit straight, keeping your back against the chair.
- Sit quietly for at least five minutes before you measure. Don’t talk, scroll your phone, or watch something that might be stressful.
- Keep your feet planted and don’t cross your legs or dangle your feet. Crossing your legs or dangling your feet can noticeably raise blood pressure.
- Don’t use the bathroom until after the reading. A full bladder can raise the reading, so empty it beforehand.
- Be ready to measure within an hour of waking up, after using the bathroom, and before eating, drinking coffee, exercising, or taking your blood pressure medication.
- If you have been diagnosed with high blood pressure or your doctor has requested monitoring, measure your blood pressure for about seven days before your medical appointment or after a medication change.
- Have a week of readings. This gives a more reliable baseline, which is more informative than any single number.

This tool can be used to protect your health. High blood pressure raises the risk of heart attack, stroke, kidney disease, and heart failure. Checking your blood pressure at home only takes a few minutes, but it can reveal a risk factor years before it causes harm.
